claims.text: Adding approximately 2–3 at% Pt/Pd by atomic layer deposition and post-deposition annealing will stabilize atomically dispersed Pt/Pd sites in the multi-principal-element catalyst.
The Pt/Pd treatment will improve low-temperature oxidation activity relative to the unmodified catalyst.
The Pt/Pd treatment will improve resistance to H2O and NO poisoning relative to the unmodified catalyst.
The Pt/Pd treatment will improve catalyst lifetime durability under transient exhaust conditions.
The initial catalyst has baseline poisoning susceptibility and undergoes degradation during accelerated aging.
The proposed deposition is performed by ALD at 200–250 °C using a total or individual Pt/Pd loading stated as 2–3 at%.
The post-ALD treatment consists of annealing at 300 °C in a mild reducing atmosphere with an anchoring strategy.
The post-deposition anchoring strategy will prevent agglomeration of the single-atom sites.
Controlled post-deposition processing will produce atomically dispersed Pt/Pd sites embedded within the alloy matrix.
Isolated Pt/Pd sites lower activation-energy barriers for oxidation reactions.
Isolated Pt/Pd sites modify the catalyst electronic structure in a way that facilitates removal of poisoning adsorbates.
Suppressing Pt/Pd sintering and agglomeration will preserve single-atom catalytic benefits during prolonged operation.
The intervention will lower the onset temperature for CO and hydrocarbon oxidation.
The intervention will reduce deactivation caused by H2O and NO.
The intervention will increase activity retention over extended lifecycle aging tests.
The unmodified catalyst has higher oxidation activation barriers than the proposed Pt/Pd-modified catalyst.
The unmodified catalyst has limited durability under transient, low-temperature exhaust conditions.
The performance improvement will be most pronounced below 150 °C in exhaust containing CO, hydrocarbons, H2O, and NO.
